hints: Notice the diode and fixed resistor are in series, so they carry the same $40\text{ mA}$ current and their p.d.s must add to $6.0\text{ V}$.
Read the diode $I-V$ graph horizontally at $I = 40\text{ mA}$ to find the p.d. $V$ across the diode itself.
Subtract the diode p.d. from $6.0\text{ V}$ to get the resistor p.d., then use $R = V/I$ with $I = 0.040\text{ A}$.
walkthrough: The series loop has current $I = 40\text{ mA} = 0.040\text{ A}$ everywhere, and by Kirchhoff's second law $V_{resistor} + V_{diode} = 6.0\text{ V}$ because internal resistance is negligible.
Find $V_{diode}$ from the $I-V$ graph. Locate $40\text{ mA}$ on the $I$-axis and read across to the curve and down to the $V$-axis.
The graph gives $V_{diode} = 1.2\text{ V}$ when $I = 40\text{ mA}$.
So the p.d. left for the fixed resistor is $V_{resistor} = 6.0 - 1.2 = 4.8\text{ V}$.
Use $R = V/I$ for the ohmic fixed resistor: $R = 4.8\text{ V} / 0.040\text{ A} = 120\text{ }\Omega$. This is option B.

options.A: This is $V/I$ for the diode alone, about $1.2\text{ V} / 0.040\text{ A}$, not the p.d. across the fixed resistor.
options.B: The resistor has $6.0 - 1.2 = 4.8\text{ V}$ across it with $0.040\text{ A}$ through it, giving $R = 4.8/0.040 = 120\text{ }\Omega$.
options.C: This uses the full $6.0\text{ V}$ across the resistor, ignoring the $1.2\text{ V}$ dropped across the diode in series.
options.D: This is too large and does not follow from $4.8\text{ V}$ across the resistor with $40\text{ mA}$ current.
